1324.title: Teaching prayer
1324.hook: a granddaughter on his shoulder, all the way through the prayer
1324.howItsDone: Muslim parents who follow the hadith in Abu Dawud begin teaching children the prayer around the age of seven, and children often learn it by praying beside their parents at home and in the mosque.

segments.voice: Yesterday: khitan, traced to Ibrahim, and your line, the way of ibrahim. Today, a parent, a child, and the prayer between them.

A man stands in prayer with a little girl up on his shoulder. When he goes down to prostrate, he sets her gently on the floor. When he stands again, he lifts her back up. Sahih al-Bukhari tells it, in paraphrase: the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, prayed while carrying his granddaughter Umamah, the daughter of his daughter Zaynab. No lecture about prayer. Just a child, riding along through it, watching every movement from up close.
screen: `A GIRL ON HIS SHOULDER.` → `DOWN TO PROSTRATE.` → `UP AGAIN WHEN HE STANDS.`

segments.voice: Start with the instruction people quote. In Sunan Abu Dawud, in paraphrase, the Prophet said: command your children to pray when they are seven years old. The same hadith goes on to speak of the age of ten with firmer words, and scholars discuss what that firmness should and shouldn't mean. But notice the order. Seven comes first, three years before the firmer words. A child isn't asked to pray as an adult does; they're given time to grow into it. Second, the Qur'an puts this in a parent's mouth. In surah Luqman, a wise father advises his son, and when he comes to prayer, in Pickthall's translation, he says: "O my dear son! Establish worship." The words are tender before they're firm. Third, the Prophet didn't treat a child as an interruption. Umamah on his shoulder, down when he prostrates, up when he stands: every movement of the prayer, seen from the closest seat in the room. Arabic has a word for what he was being: a qudwah, an example to follow. A child copies the bow before understanding it, and learns the words from hearing them said nearby. Fourth, the line that ties it together. The Qur'an tells the Prophet, in Pickthall's words: "And enjoin upon thy people worship, and be constant therein." Tell others, and keep doing it yourself. The instruction and the example travel together, and without the example, the instruction has nothing to point to.
screen: `PRAY AT SEVEN: YEARS TO GROW INTO IT.` · `O MY DEAR SON! ESTABLISH WORSHIP.` · `UMAMAH ON HIS SHOULDER.` · `ENJOIN IT, AND BE CONSTANT.`

segments.voice: If you pray and there's a child in your life, picture the next prayer you could let them watch, or join, or just sit beside, with no correcting. If there's no child near you, remember the first person you watched do something devoted, pray, read, give, light a candle, and what the small one watching took away.
Teaching prayer. Children are told to pray from seven, and they learn it beside someone who prays. Today's word.
Your line: teach by praying. The example goes first, and the words follow it. Until tomorrow.

1325.title: The first khatm
1325.hook: the last page, a finger under the line, a family pretending not to listen
1325.howItsDone: In some Muslim communities, a child who finishes reading the whole Qur'an for the first time is honored with a gathering, where the child recites the closing surahs and the family thanks the teacher; the customs and names vary by culture.

segments.voice: Yesterday: teaching prayer, and your line, teach by praying. Today, the day a child reaches the last page.

A child sits cross-legged with a big book on a little wooden stand, a finger moving under the lines, voice careful. The teacher leans in. The family is in the doorway, pretending not to listen. It's the last page. A few short surahs left, then the final line of al-Nas, and it's done: the whole Qur'an, read through, out loud. In some homes and mosques, that moment gets a party: new clothes, sweets, guests, the child reading the closing surahs in front of everyone.
screen: `A FINGER UNDER THE LINE.` → `THE LAST PAGE.` → `THE WHOLE BOOK, READ THROUGH.`

segments.voice: Khatm means a completion: a full reading of the Qur'an, from the opening to the end. Adults do it too, alone or together, sometimes over a single month. But a child's first khatm can take years of small daily lessons to reach. Why celebrate it? A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase: the best of you are those who learn the Qur'an and teach it. The child has learned, and someone, a parent, a teacher, an imam, has taught. A khatm party honors both halves of that sentence at once. Second, the struggle counts. In Bukhari and Muslim, in paraphrase: the one who is skilled at reciting the Qur'an is with the noble, righteous scribes, and the one who recites it haltingly, finding it hard, has a double reward. Hear that from the child's side. Every stumble over a long word wasn't wasted; in this hadith, the struggling reader is the one promised two rewards. Third, the book says it can be carried. In surah al-Qamar, in Pickthall's translation: "And in truth We have made the Qur'an easy to remember." A child at a little stand, closing the last page, is that verse in a living room. Fourth, it doesn't really end. Some families mark the khatm by having the child turn straight back to the beginning and read al-Fatiha again, right there. Finish, and start again. The celebration isn't for being done. It's for being on the way.
screen: `LEARN IT AND TEACH IT.` · `THE HALTING READER: A DOUBLE REWARD.` · `EASY TO REMEMBER.` · `FINISH, AND START AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a child who has finished something lately, a book, a school year, the alphabet, or remember your own first finish and who was there for it. Think of words that honor the work, not just the result: I saw how hard you worked. If you pray, thank Allah for their learning in your own words; if not, just let yourself be glad for them.
The first khatm. A child's first complete reading of the Qur'an, and the celebration some families give it. Today's word.
Your line: a child finishes. And then, right there, starts again. Same time tomorrow.

1326.title: Coming of age
1326.hook: the pen is lifted from the child, until one day it isn't
1326.howItsDone: In Islamic law, a person becomes mukallaf at maturity, and from then on prayer, fasting and the other duties are required of them; before that, children are encouraged to practice and their good deeds are welcomed.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the first khatm, and your line, a child finishes. Today the child grows up, and something quietly changes.

For years a child prays beside a parent, copies the bows, maybe tries a half-day fast in Ramadan to see what it's like. All of it is real, and all of it is welcome. And yet, in Islamic teaching, there's a line waiting up ahead. One day, with no ceremony required, the child crosses it. A hadith describes the time before that line with a striking picture: the pen is lifted.
screen: `PRAYING BESIDE A PARENT.` → `A LINE WAITING UP AHEAD.` → `THE PEN IS LIFTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the hadith, in Sunan Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi, in paraphrase: the pen is lifted from three. From the sleeper until he wakes, from the child until he reaches maturity, and from the one who has lost his reason until he recovers it. Commentators read the pen as the one that records a person's deeds against them. Before maturity, nothing is yet written against a child. Childhood is protected time. But protected isn't empty. In Sahih Muslim, in paraphrase, a woman on the pilgrimage lifts up a small child and asks the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: does he have a Hajj? He answers: yes, and you have a reward. A child's good deeds are welcomed. Second, the word. Taklif means being given a charge, a responsibility. A person who has reached it is called mukallaf: one who is now responsible. Scholars set out the signs of maturity, and the schools differ on the details, but the idea is shared: at maturity, the duties begin. Prayer, fasting, the rest. Now it counts. Third, the charge comes with a limit. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation: "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope." In Arabic, that verse's verb is yukallifu, from the same root as taklif. The charge and its limit, in one sentence. Fourth, look back at the years before. The khatm, the prayers beside a parent, the half fasts: none of it was required. It was practice, freely given. Taklif doesn't erase that. It builds on it. The child who already knows the movements walks into responsibility already holding them.
screen: `THE PEN IS LIFTED FROM THREE.` · `TAKLIF: GIVEN A CHARGE.` · `NOT BEYOND ITS SCOPE.` · `PRACTICE BECOMES RESPONSIBILITY.`

segments.voice: Recall a moment when something in your life started to count, a first job, a key of your own, a promise that was yours to keep, and name one responsibility you carry now that fits you, not one beyond your scope. Then let this part of the path pass by: the call in the ear, the date, the name, the 'aqiqah, the hair, khitan, prayer at seven, the khatm, and now taklif. A whole childhood.
Taklif. Being given a charge: at maturity, the duties of the faith begin, and none beyond a soul's scope. Today's word.
Your line: now it counts. A charge, and never one beyond your scope. Rest well, and come back tomorrow.

1327.title: Choosing a spouse
1327.hook: four honest reasons people marry, and the one a hadith puts first
1327.howItsDone: Muslims looking for a spouse, and their families, cite the hadith in Bukhari and Tirmidhi to put faith and character ahead of wealth, family standing and looks.

segments.voice: Yesterday: taklif, and your line, now it counts. The child is grown, and a new part of the path begins: marriage and home.

A list, written before anyone has met. Steady income? Good family? Attractive? Gets along with my mother? These days some of that list lives inside apps, as filters you can slide up and down. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari makes a list like this too, and it's surprisingly frank about it. It doesn't pretend people marry for spiritual reasons alone. It names four reasons, out loud, and then it points at one of them and says: that one.
screen: `A LIST, BEFORE ANYONE MEETS.` → `FOUR REASONS, NAMED OUT LOUD.` → `THEN: THAT ONE.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in paraphrase. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said: a woman is married for four things: her wealth, her family standing, her beauty, and her religion. Choose the one with religion, and you will prosper. Then he adds a sharp Arabic phrase, taribat yadak, which literally means may your hands be covered in dust. Here it works like a nudge: pay attention, get this one right. Notice what the hadith doesn't do. It doesn't call wealth, family or beauty bad. It names them plainly; it just won't let them sit at the top of the list. Second, character. A hadith in Jami' at-Tirmidhi speaks to a family receiving a proposal, in paraphrase: if someone comes to you whose religion and character please you, then marry. The Arabic for character is khuluq: the way a person actually is, on a bad day, when nobody's grading them. Put the two side by side and you have today's line: faith and character first. Third, it runs both ways. One hadith speaks about choosing a wife, the other about accepting a husband. The same measure falls on both sides. Fourth, what that looks like up close. Not a title, not how loudly someone talks about religion. It shows in small things: how someone treats the person serving their food, whether they keep a promise that cost them something, how they speak about their parents, whether they keep their prayers on an ordinary weekday. The filters ask what someone has. These two hadith ask who someone is.
screen: `WEALTH, FAMILY, BEAUTY, RELIGION.` · `CHOOSE RELIGION: TARIBAT YADAK.` · `RELIGION AND CHARACTER PLEASE YOU.` · `WHO SOMEONE IS, NOT WHAT THEY HAVE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose character you trust: not the most impressive person you know, the most dependable. What do they actually do, keep their word, speak kindly of people who aren't in the room? Then turn it around gently: where does your own character already show like that, and if you pray, ask for good character in your own words.
Choosing a spouse. Four reasons people marry, named honestly, and two put first: faith and character. Today's word.
Your line: character first. Who someone is, before what they have. A new part of the path, begun.

1328.title: Asking permission
1328.hook: a young woman brings a complaint about her own father's arrangement
1328.howItsDone: Muslims cite these hadith for a bride's consent: she is asked before the contract, and the schools set out the role of her guardian, the wali, in different ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday: choosing a spouse, and your line, character first. Today, the question nobody in a marriage gets to skip.

A woman comes to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, with a complaint about her own father. He has married her to a man, and she didn't want it. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps her name: Khansa' bint Khidham. Her case comes down to a plain question: does a marriage made over her refusal stand? The father has made his decision. And she has come to the one person whose answer will settle it.
screen: `A COMPLAINT ABOUT HER FATHER.` → `KHANSA' BINT KHIDHAM.` → `DOES IT STAND?`

segments.voice: The report in Bukhari, in paraphrase: her father married her off while she disliked it, she came to the Messenger of Allah, and he annulled the marriage. A father's arrangement didn't override her refusal. Second, the rule behind the story. Another hadith in Bukhari, in paraphrase: a woman who has been married before is not to be married until she is consulted, and a woman who has never married, not until her permission is asked. The companions asked: how is her permission given? In one version, 'A'ishah adds: but she is shy. And the Prophet answered: her silence. That's a careful detail. Silence isn't the goal. The hadith makes room for a shy bride without letting anyone skip her. She is asked, and her answer, even a quiet one, is the answer. And Khansa's story shows that a clear no ends it. Third, the word. In Arabic, permission is idhn. Think of a door. In surah al-Nur, the Qur'an says, in paraphrase, that if you find no one home, you don't go in until you've been given permission. A marriage, like a house, isn't entered without being let in. Fourth, the schools. Muslim scholars discuss the role of the bride's guardian, the wali, and the schools differ on the details. But beneath the details, these two hadith hold one line in place: she is asked, and her answer counts.

segments.voice: Think of a decision coming up that touches someone else: a plan you'd make for them, a photo you'd post of them, a favor you'd volunteer them for. Picture yourself asking first, then waiting for the answer without leaning on it: a question, and a pause long enough for the reply.
Asking permission. A bride is asked before her marriage, and her no is honored. Today's word.
Your line: her consent. Even a shy yes is hers to give. That one's in the books.

1329.title: The nikah ceremony
1329.hook: a sermon, an offer and an acceptance, witnesses, and a blessing passed around the room
1329.howItsDone: A Muslim marriage is a contract (nikah) made by offer and acceptance before witnesses, with a mahr for the bride, often opened by a short sermon; guests may congratulate the couple with "barakallahu lakuma".

segments.voice: Yesterday: asking permission, and your line, her consent. She has been asked, and she has said yes. Today, the wedding itself.

The room might be a mosque, a living room, or a rented hall with too many folding chairs. The clothes change from country to country; the food changes even more. But underneath all of it, the nikah itself is short, and its main pieces are few. A brief sermon. An offer, and an acceptance. Witnesses who hear it. And then a short line goes around the room, said again and again to the couple, by aunts, friends and strangers.
screen: `A MOSQUE, A LIVING ROOM, A HALL.` → `SHORT, UNDER ALL OF IT.` → `A LINE GOES AROUND THE ROOM.`

segments.voice: First, the sermon. Tradition opens the nikah with a short sermon the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, taught, reported in Sunan Abu Dawud: praise of God, and verses of the Qur'an about mindfulness of God and speaking straight. One of them, from surah al-Nisa, reminds everyone that all people were created from a single soul, and its mate from it. A wedding begins by remembering where every couple comes from. Second, the offer and the acceptance: in Arabic, ijab and qabul. One side offers, the other accepts, in clear words. It's a contract, an 'aqd. And the Qur'an asks that the bride receive a gift, the mahr. In Pickthall's translation: "And give unto the women (whom ye marry) free gift of their marriage portions." The gift is hers. Third, the witnesses. A nikah isn't a secret. The schools of law set out the conditions, the witnesses and the role of the bride's guardian, and they differ on the details. But the shape is public: people hear it, and can say they heard it. Fourth, the blessing. In Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi, when the Prophet congratulated someone on a marriage, he would say, in paraphrase: may Allah bless you, and send blessing upon you, and bring you together in goodness. At weddings you may hear a short form of it: barakallahu lakuma, may Allah bless you both. Lakuma means you two. The blessing is spoken to the pair, together.
screen: `A SERMON: FROM A SINGLE SOUL.` · `IJAB AND QABUL, AND THE MAHR.` · `WITNESSES: A NIKAH IS PUBLIC.` · `BARAKALLAHU LAKUMA.`

segments.voice: Say it slowly, a piece at a time: barakallahu, lakuma, barakallahu lakuma, may Allah bless you both. Bring to mind a couple, newly married or married for decades, and if you pray, hold them in mind as you say it. If you don't, just learn the sound of it, so the next time you hear it at a wedding, you'll know it's a blessing being passed around the room.

1330.title: Tranquillity in marriage
1330.hook: a door closes at the end of the day, and a verse about what waits behind it
1330.howItsDone: Muslims read Qur'an 30:21 as describing the purpose of marriage: rest and calm with one another, with love and mercy between spouses, and the verse is recited or quoted at some weddings and in marriage advice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the nikah, and your line, barakallahu lakuma. The guests have gone home. Today, the marriage, and a verse about what it's for.

A door closes at the end of a long day. Keys in the bowl. Shoes off. For some people, that click of the lock is the best sound of the day. For others, it's the start of a second shift, or a second argument. The Qur'an has a verse about the people behind that door. It isn't about the wedding day; some readers hear in it an ordinary evening, years in. It's in surah al-Rum, and it calls the making of spouses one of God's signs.
screen: `A DOOR CLOSES.` → `THE BEST SOUND, OR A SECOND SHIFT.` → `ONE OF HIS SIGNS.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's translation: "And of His signs is this: He created for you helpmeets from yourselves that ye might find rest in them, and He ordained between you love and mercy." Four things sit inside that sentence. First, from yourselves. A spouse isn't a creature of another kind: same nature, same origin, the single soul the nikah sermon remembered yesterday. Second, rest. Pickthall says find rest; other English translations say dwell in tranquillity, which is today's line. The Arabic is li-taskunu: that you may settle, be still, be at peace with. The verse doesn't say marriage is for excitement, or status. It says: so that you can settle. Third, love and mercy, in Arabic mawaddah and rahmah. And notice the verb: He ordained them, placed them between you. They're given before they're earned; the couple's part is to keep them there. Some readers notice the verse names both, as if mercy carries the house on the days love is tired. Fourth, a picture from another surah. In al-Baqarah, Pickthall's translation says of husbands and wives: "They are raiment for you and ye are raiment for them." Clothing: close to the skin, warm, covering what needs covering, worn every single day. Put the two verses together and the sign isn't a grand gesture. It's the evening, when the door clicks shut, and the house is a place to rest.
screen: `FROM YOURSELVES.` · `THAT YE MIGHT FIND REST IN THEM.` · `LOVE AND MERCY, PLACED BETWEEN.` · `RAIMENT FOR EACH OTHER.`

segments.voice: Picture walking through your own door tonight, and taking one breath at the threshold before you put anything down. Choose one thing to leave outside, a tone, a complaint, and one thing to bring in, a greeting, a question, a cup of tea for someone. Picture the room a little quieter because of it.

Your line: dwell in tranquillity. Love, and mercy for the days love is tired. Peace in your home tonight.
